correctness.rationale: The proof derives the exact positive two-site killed resolvent and renewal flux ratio; positive determinant ensures well-defined probabilities. Rearrangement yields P_R>1/2 iff A<H_B(t), with H_B(0)=B/(1+B) and H_B(infty)=0. For B>1, its derivative at zero is B(B-1)/(1+B)^2>0. For 0<B<=1, the affine K(B,t) is strictly negative at B=0 and B=1 for every t>0, where the B=1 bound follows t<sinh t and the exact positive remainder (1-q)(1-q^2)^2/q. The explicit A=11/10,B=100 witness uses ln(2)>2/3, giving strict two-crossing brackets. The standalone checker independently solves the resolvent at 175 cases; it is supplementary, not an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The foundational 2013 paper treats one imperfect absorber; the closest 2019 paper supplies general two-defect resolvent and perfect two-target splitting, so formula (1) itself is prior implied. The additional new claim is the global iff B>1 existence condition and complete sharp interval B/(1+B)<A<C(B), proved by a global inequality not stated in the inspected closest text. Relevant 2020–2025 primary literature on broader target competition, finite partially absorbing targets and general selectivity has been compared; the incomplete specialized literature remains a genuine residual priority risk.
residual_risks: Giuggioli et al. (2019) already gives a broader forward two-defect Green-function solution, implying the exact capture odds here; originality is confined to the proved global iff phase boundary and reentrance window.
The literature search is finite and a specialized unlocated prior result may already derive the same iff threshold.
The full text of Pal–Prasad (2018) was not materially inspected; its abstract describes perfectly absorbing endpoints, but no noncoverage claim about all its content is inferred.
The theorem is confined to the 1:2 point-target placement and does not prove exactly two (rather than at least two) crossings.

value.rationale: The reentrant majority phenomenon is a natural observable about *which* imperfect target ultimately captures a reset Brownian searcher, distinct from optimizing mean time. An exact sharp far-reactivity feasibility threshold B=1 and a complete strict near-reactivity phase window reveal why the farther site can prevail only at intermediate reset intensities even though it loses at both endpoint regimes. The global obstruction when B<=1 requires a substantive nonlocal inequality, rather than a routine parameter substitution or isolated numerical example.
